label: Skills
title: Skills
subtitle: A skill is a reusable set of instructions that changes how an agent approaches a task — its tone, methodology, format, or step-by-step procedure. Where a knowledge base gives an agent facts to look up, a skill gives an agent a way of working to follow whenever it is active.

subsections.title: What Is a Skill?
subsections.description: Skills are Markdown files that get injected directly into an agent's instructions when active. A concrete example: an "Academic Writing" skill might tell the agent to always structure responses with an abstract, introduction, methodology, and conclusion; to cite sources inline using APA format; to avoid first-person language; and to flag any claim it cannot support with a reference. Another example: a "Python Code Review" skill might instruct the agent to check for type hints on all function signatures, flag bare except clauses, and always suggest a test case alongside any proposed fix. Once you create a skill and assign it to an agent, that agent applies those rules to every message — you do not have to repeat the instructions each time.
subsections.mediaCaption: A skill card in the Skills tab showing name, description, keywords, and enabled status

subsections.title: Built-in Skills
subsections.description: InnoviumAI ships a few ready-made skills you can assign without writing any Markdown. "innovium-docs" is the platform's own documentation, assigned to the PI agent by default, so an agent can answer questions about the app it is running inside. Others — such as "latex-documents" for TII-templated documents — cover common workflows. Built-in skills appear in the Skills tab alongside your own and can be enabled, disabled, or copied as a starting point for a customised version.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Skills tab listing built-in skills like innovium-docs alongside user-created skills

subsections.title: Creating a Skill
subsections.description: Go to Settings and open the Skills tab. Click Create Skill to open the editor. Fill in the Name field using lowercase letters and hyphens (for example, "python-best-practices" or "formal-report-writing") — this becomes the skill's unique identifier. Write a short Description explaining what the skill does. Then write the Skill Instructions in the large Markdown text area — these are the rules the agent will follow, supporting any Markdown formatting including headings, bullet lists, and code blocks. Switch the toggle above the text area to Preview to see the instructions rendered, and back to Edit to keep writing. Optionally add Keywords (short tags like "python" or "academic") used by the auto-discovery feature. Click Create to save. The skill is stored in your ~/.innovium-ai/files/global/skills folder as a Markdown file, so you can also edit it directly in a text editor.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Create Skill dialog with the name, description, keywords, and Markdown instruction fields filled in

subsections.title: When to Use a Skill vs Other Options
subsections.description: Use a skill when you have a methodology, a style rule, or a step-by-step procedure that should apply every time an agent works on a certain type of task — and that you would otherwise have to retype into every new conversation. Use a knowledge base when you have documents or data the agent needs to look facts up from. Use neither when the instruction is truly one-off: just say it in the message. The practical rule: if you have typed the same paragraph of instructions into three different conversations, it belongs in a skill. If you have pasted the same document three times, it belongs in a knowledge base. Avoid putting large blocks of reference content directly into a skill — that is what a knowledge base is for — because skill content is injected into the prompt on every message and will consume context window space even when it is not needed.
subsections.mediaCaption: Side-by-side comparison: the Skills tab for methodology rules and the Knowledge Base dialog for documents

subsections.title: Auto-Activation
subsections.description: Each agent has an Auto-discover toggle in its settings. When enabled, InnoviumAI scores all enabled skills against the content of each incoming message using keyword and description matching, then automatically includes the top matching skills in the agent's context — up to three additional skills beyond any you have manually assigned. This is useful when you have a library of specialist skills and do not want to manually switch them on for every project: ask about a Python bug and the "python-best-practices" skill activates; ask for a report draft and "formal-report-writing" activates instead. Manual assignment is the safer starting point — it gives you predictable behaviour. Switch to auto-discovery once you have several skills and find yourself frequently changing which ones are active.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Auto-discover toggle in an agent's Skills settings alongside manually assigned skill cards

subsections.title: Sharing a Skill with a Colleague
subsections.description: A skill you wrote can go straight to someone else in your profile. Open Settings, go to the Skills tab, and click the share icon on the skill's card — it appears on skills you created and on marketplace skills you have edited. The dialog is titled "Share Skill:" followed by the skill's name, and it opens on "Share with User". Type a name or an email address into "Search users in your profile" to pick the person, add an optional note saying why you are sending it, and click Share. Nothing is installed behind their back: the skill arrives as a card in their notifications panel naming the skill and who sent it, and they click View to see the sender, the time, and your note before choosing Accept, Reject, or Remind Me Later. For a skill you wrote yourself and have not published, accepting writes it onto their machine as a copy of their own, which they can then read, edit, disable, or delete like any skill they wrote themselves. A skill's name is also its identity, so it cannot land on a machine that already holds a skill of that name — which is the case for one you edited after downloading it, and for one of your own once it has been published and downloaded across the profile. Your colleague's Accept then fails with an error, and the share stays in their notifications panel so nothing is lost. To hand on changes to a skill the catalog already holds, propose them to your profile instead.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Share Skill dialog on the Share with User route, with a recipient picked from the profile search

subsections.title: Proposing a Skill to Your Profile or Organisation
subsections.description: The same dialog offers two routes that go through review instead of straight to a person. "Share with Profile" sends the skill to the people who manage your profile, so it can become a default for everyone in it. "Share with Organization" aims it at the organisation-wide catalog, where an administrator decides instead; it is offered only for a skill you wrote from scratch, not for one you edited after downloading it. The button at the bottom names the outcome: Publish for a skill of your own, and Propose when you are offering your changes to a skill that came from the catalog — which is how an improvement to a downloaded skill reaches the person who curates it. Nobody else in your profile sees the skill until it is approved. The reviewer opens your submission under Proposals in the dashboard and reads the skill itself, not just its name; when you are changing something that already exists, they get a line-by-line diff of what you altered, with a Diff/Full toggle for switching between your changes and the whole thing. Approve puts the skill in front of everyone in the profile at their next sync, and Reject leaves the skill yours to fix and send again. On a skill you published in full the reviewer can also leave a note explaining the decision; a proposed change is approved or rejected without one. The decision and any note live in the dashboard for now; the app does not yet tell you either way, so ask a manager of your profile where a submission stands. The three rules that follow belong to Publish, because only a published skill takes a name in the catalog. Sending a rejected skill again keeps the name it already has: your fixed version replaces the rejected submission rather than filing a second one, so hold on to the name while you work. Renaming answers a different message — when the catalog already holds a skill under that name, the submission is refused and the message usually names a variation that is free, so rename the skill as suggested and publish again. A skill still waiting in the queue is refused too, with a message saying it is already awaiting review. A Propose is checked none of those ways, so send it once and wait: proposing the same change again files a second request alongside the first, and a rejected proposal holds no name for you to keep.
subsections.mediaCaption: The Share Skill dialog on the Share with Profile route, explaining that a manager reviews the submission before anyone else sees it
